title: Solo dev, 8 months in: how I got consistent sprite sheets for ~50 possessable creatures with AI, and where it failed. Chapter 1 of my action-RPG is free in the browser
author: Devolik13
selftext:
The game: you have no body. You possess creatures — hare, wolf, bandit, elemental — and each one teaches you a skill that stays with you forever. Chapter 1 has \~50 "teacher" bodies, so the pipeline question from day one was: how do I get 50 animated characters as one person?



What worked. Sprite sheets come from AutoSprite: I describe the creature, get a master sheet with idle/walk/death rows in four directions, then repack it myself into the engine's 7-row format. The repacking is where the real work is — the generator's rows come out in a different order every time, and some rows are drawn at a different scale (the "idle facing camera" of my old bear was visibly smaller than its walk). I ended up with a packer that scales per row and even per frame range, and a rule I learned the hard way: never trust the row order, check with your eyes. Hovering creatures (elementals) don't get walk animations at all — the walk rows are copies of idle, and the engine just keeps the cycle running on turn instead of restarting it.



What didn't. I tried going 3D: a GLB of my orc chief rigged with Mixamo, rendered to sheets in headless Chromium with three.js. Movement was smoother — frames actually agreed with each other — but the generated model lost what made the drawn version good: thinner, fewer details. I kept the drawn sheets. Maybe someone here has cracked drawn-look-to-3D better than I did?



Icons and sound were the other volume problem: \~130 spell icons, \~70 status icons, \~70 achievement badges and \~50 item icons, all generated in style batches and sliced from sheets by script. For sound effects I use ElevenLabs' SFX model — about 70 of them — and the one recipe that mattered: describe the process and the materials ("flame catching on dry branches, whoosh plus crackle"), never the word "hit" or "impact" — those always come back as a metallic anvil clang. Generate 2–3 seconds, trim to the first second yourself.



Voice is ElevenLabs Voice Design, not cloning — about 200 lines in chapter 1, two languages, each villager with a designed voice. The thing nobody tells you: a line like "{name}, come here" can't be one file when the name depends on which body the player wears. I write those lines name-free and let the subtitle carry it. Music is Suno.



Code is Phaser 3 + TypeScript, written with Claude Code — and this is where AI pulled the most weight. There are 117 spells and skills across 15 weapons and 5 magic schools, and the rule I set early was "one implementation per effect": a fire wall or a wind blade has to behave identically whether the player, a monster or the player's golem casts it. Claude built that unified layer, and a build-time audit script that fails the build if a creature gets a spell the shared layer can't execute — so the pile can't silently rot. Design, balance, quests and the story are mine, and that's still most of the hours.



The clip is a fight at a farmstead — the two mages are bodies the player possessed earlier, holding against goblin waves.



Free, runs in the browser (Windows build too): [https://devolikin.itch.io/essence-the-other-wave](https://devolikin.itch.io/essence-the-other-wave)



Curious what sheet-consistency tricks others use — the per-row scale hack feels like it shouldn't be necessary.

comments.author: Dramatic_Leopard679
comments.body: Well done and interesting read. Thanks!

replies.author: Devolik13
replies.body: Thanks! If you try it — the first 10 minutes are the real test, curious whether the "possess things" rule lands without explanation.

comments.author: cheyumaama
comments.body: It looks pretty AI made for something you spent 8 months on

replies.author: Devolik13
replies.body: Fair — the look is the generated part, and it shows. The months went into what the art sits on: 117 skills that behave identically for the player, monsters and the golem, \~50 body quests, the ecosystem, two-language voice, and a lot of repacking those sheets by hand. If there's a specific spot where it reads "AI-made" in a bad way, I'd genuinely like to know which — consistency is exactly the fight I'm losing slowest.

replies.author: cheyumaama
replies.body: Great mechanics and all, but I'd invest more time to make it look better. The average gamer isn't going to play your game if it doesn't grasp their attention with its visuals and hold them so that they're interested in exploring the rest of your world

replies.author: Devolik13
replies.body: Agreed, and thanks for saying it straight — "great mechanics, looks AI-made" is the exact gap I need to close before the Steam page. One question, since you've got fresh eyes: what would you fix first — the characters, the environment, or the UI? From the inside I can't tell which one is doing the most damage.

replies.author: cheyumaama
replies.body: The characters look fine to my eyes and the UI is decent too except for the gold font that AI loves to use for some reason. I'd mostly work on the environment and the attack graphics from the video you've posted. Attack graphics would get my most attention since they are a big part of what would draw someone in and keep them hooked

replies.author: Devolik13
replies.body: That's exactly the kind of answer I was hoping for — thank you. Attack VFX first, then environment; and I'll look at that gold font with fresh eyes, I'd stopped seeing it. Appreciate you taking the time.

replies.author: cheyumaama
replies.body: Of course man. Happy to help
